name: 돌 단 앞 턱(가운데, 1칸) (dais riser stone)
label: atlas_biome_interior/plus/dais riser stone

surfaces.part: dais riser stone face (top light band, rows 4-6 graded)
stone riser front face with brick joints

answer.evidence: The tile is opaque on rows 4-15 at full width 16, with rows 0-3 transparent. Rows 4-6 form a light-to-mid gradient band (L 206, 171, 150), which could be a lit top edge or a bevel. There is no clear front-edge line followed by an eave shadow. Rows 7-15 are a brick-joint front face with dark mortar lines at rows 10 and 14 and short vertical joints. The riser is mainly a vertical face, and the light band is a 3-row highlight or bevel rather than a clear horizontal top surface. It reads as a front elevation of a stone riser, as expected for a riser tile in terrain, where the dais top is a separate tile.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a one-tile stone riser made of two rows of bricks with a light top edge, mortar lines and a darker underside. It shows about 5 distinct lightness steps. Measured facts: 6 visible tones per tile against 7 for the paving reference and 3 for the grass reference, and 0% near-flat coverage, the same as both references. Only 33% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, against 80% for the paving reference, so the outline is a mix of tinted and neutral tones rather than a uniform black sticker line. The brick faces carry some variation, but the texture is cleaner and sparser than the dense cobble grain of the paving reference. For a small single-tile riser that is acceptable, and it sits close to the reference on the primary facts.

surfaces.part: stone front face with two brick courses

answer.evidence: The tile is a full-width block, 16px wide over rows 4-15. Rows 4-6 step from light (L=206, 171, 150) toward the face tone (L=124). This reads as a bevel or highlight rim of about 2-3 rows, with no distinct front-edge line and no eave shadow. Rows 7-15 are a vertical stone face with mortar lines at rows 10 and 14 and joint marks, which gives a flat front elevation. There is no ellipse, no sloped plane and no visible contents, so no real horizontal top surface is shown.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a single small grey stone riser: two courses of bricks with light top edges and dark mortar lines. The measured facts are close to the paving reference: 6 visible tones against 7, and 0% near-flat coverage. Raw colours are 6 against 7, so the palette is similarly small. The weaknesses show by eye. The brick faces are smooth and mostly one mid-grey, without the stone-by-stone speckle and shading of the cobbled reference. Only about 5 lightness steps are readable against the reference's 6. Dark edge pixels are 33% neutral, so the outline is mixed and the piece leans slightly toward a clean, sticker-like block. It is clean and no 5x5 area is flat, but it reads thinner and flatter than the reference paving. Since a doubtful piece should fail, it fails.

There is no distinct front-edge line and no eave shadow, so this is a bevel highlight or rim of 1-3 rows, not a horizontal top surface. Below it are two stone courses divided by dark mortar lines at rows 10 and 14, with vertical joints at x=4 and x=11, and a dark base at row 15. The whole piece is a vertical riser face, which suits a terrain tile such as a dais front lip, but it shows no top plane.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a single small riser tile of brick-laid grey stone. It has a light top lip, mid-grey stone faces and dark mortar joints, about 5 lightness steps. It measures 6 visible tones per tile against 7 for the paving reference, and 3 for the grass reference. Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references, so there is no large flat fill. Only 33% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, against 80% for the paving reference, so the joints lean toward a tinted stone tone rather than a uniform black sticker line. It is simpler than the cobble paving, which shades each stone individually, and the stone faces are less speckled. For a one-tile riser edge this is still comparable in tone count and structure and would sit acceptably beside the reference.

answer.evidence: The tile is 16 px wide and fully opaque on rows 4-15. Rows 4-6 are a bright-to-mid gradient (L 206, 171, 150) that works as a bevel highlight on the riser's top edge. It is not a horizontal surface: no front-edge line follows it and no eave shadow sits below it. Row 6 goes straight to the face tone (L 124) on row 7. Below that is a flat vertical stone wall in two courses. Row 10 (L 76) is a dark joint, and row 11 is a light row at the top of the lower course. Short dark vertical mortar joints sit in rows 7-9 and 12-13. Rows 14-15 are a dark base shadow. There is no ellipse, no sloped plane and no contents. This is a vertical riser face with no readable top plane, so it reads as front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a one-tile stone riser of stacked bricks. It has a light top-edge highlight, a mid-gray face, darker lower edges and dark mortar joints, which gives about 5 lightness steps against roughly 6-7 in the paving reference. It measures 6 visible tones per tile against 7 for the paving reference, with 0% near-flat coverage, so there are no large flat fills. The dark edge pixels are only 33% neutral, so the outline leans partly toward tinted tones. Stone is naturally gray, and the paving reference itself is 80% neutral, so this does not read as a black sticker outline. The brick faces carry less per-stone grain than the cobbled paving, so density is slightly lower, but a careful artist would accept it beside the reference as a riser piece.
